title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: The Ring and the Dust

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close, unhurried look at one of the strangest and most rewarding novels in the English language.
Our Mutual Friend was Dickens's last completed novel, and it is — by some distance — his most labyrinthine.
It begins with a body pulled from the Thames and ends with a reckoning that unmasks half a dozen identities.
In between, Dickens gives us dust mounds, forged wills, a doll's dressmaker who sees visions, and a society so obsessed with money it can barely speak of anything else.
I'm joined today by three extraordinary readers, each of whom brings a completely different set of tools to the novel.

Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose great passion is the craft beneath the surface — the sentence architecture, the image doing ten times the work it seems to be doing.
If anyone is going to show us why a single clause in this novel is a small masterpiece, it's Eleanor.
Dr. Daniel Rosen reads novels as anatomies of power — the way institutions, money, and class shape every relationship on the page.
He has a gift for making you see just how politically charged Dickens's comedy really is, and he's never less than bracing.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has been returning to it ever since.
She brings the most precious thing: the reader's ear — the instinct for what is moving, what is funny, what makes you stop and re-read a line at midnight.
We begin where the novel's deepest questions begin: with wealth, with what it does to people, and with the rare souls it cannot buy.
What strikes me first, every time I come back to this novel, is how precisely Dickens locates the moral centre in characters the plot seems designed to marginalise.
Take the Boffins — a dustman and his wife, servants their whole lives, apparently minor figures in the inheritance plot.
And yet Dickens gives us this extraordinary passage explaining why old John Harmon — the dead Jailer of Harmony Jail, as Dickens calls him — left them in his will.
The explanation is almost paradoxical: he trusted them precisely because he had raged at them and could not break them.
Dickens writes that — and I want to read this exactly —
"he had perceived the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt."
That word — powerlessness — applied to wealth, in a novel entirely about the power of wealth, is doing enormous work.
Dickens is telling us, from very early on, that the novel's real currency is moral integrity — and it can't be minted.
Eleanor's right that the word powerlessness is startling — but I want to press on what the passage actually reveals about old Harmon's psychology.
Dickens says he mistrusted all who bore any resemblance to himself.
"sorely indeed he did mistrust all who bore any resemblance to himself"
That is a devastating psychological observation, slipped in almost parenthetically.
The rich man's paranoia about being robbed is, at its root, a projection — he knows what he himself would do if the positions were reversed.
What the Boffins represent isn't simply virtue — they represent people who have not yet been deformed by the system that deformed him.
And the tragedy, which the novel traces with extraordinary precision, is whether they can stay that way once the money arrives.
What moves me about that passage is the phrase the dead Jailer of Harmony Jail.
Harmony Jail — the family home, the place that should be warm, renamed as a prison.
And old Harmon is its jailer even in death — his will reaches out like locked bars from beyond the grave.
But what I keep coming back to — and this is where the novel's tenderness lives for me — is Jenny Wren and Lizzie.
There's a moment between them that is almost shockingly simple in its physical description.
Just this:
"she turned again, and folded them round Lizzie's neck, and rocked herself on Lizzie's breast."
In a novel full of schemes and dust and drowned men, that sentence lands like something from a different register entirely.
It's the novel breathing, for just a moment.
Caroline, I'm so glad you read that aloud — because it really doesn't work until you hear it.
The verb rocked — she is a child being comforted, and a woman offering comfort, simultaneously.
Jenny Wren's whole character is built on that kind of doubling — the one who needs protecting, who also protects.
And Dickens gets that into three verbs: turned, folded, rocked.
And by the end of the novel, that tenderness between Lizzie and Jenny is put in sharp contrast with what Harmon finally does say about the Boffins.
When John Harmon confronts Wegg, he delivers what is essentially a speech of absolute moral debt.
He says — and the parenthesis here is everything —
"I owe everything I possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness, goodness (there are no words to satisfy me) of Mr and Mrs Boffin."
There are no words to satisfy me — that is Dickens admitting that the novel's moral vocabulary is insufficient for what the Boffins are.
That's a novelist breaking his own frame, in the best possible way.
That phrase — there are no words to satisfy me — might be the most honest sentence in the novel.
And it sets up everything we want to explore today: the limits of language, the limits of money, and the people this novel can't quite contain.
Coming up, we turn to the Thames — the river that starts the novel's chain of death and resurrection — and what Dickens does with water as a moral element.

segments.title: Money and Moral Corruption: The Boffin Paradox

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's great final completed novel apart — carefully, lovingly, and without mercy.
I'm your host, and today we're diving into one of the novel's most persistent obsessions: the way money corrodes, disguises, and ultimately reveals character.
We're calling this segment The Boffin Paradox — the question of what wealth does to good people, and what it unmasks in bad ones.
With me today are three guests who know this novel deeply and see it quite differently from one another.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens above all as a craftsman — she'll be watching the architecture, the sentences, the images.
Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every institution in the novel as a mechanism of class power — he earns his anger with evidence.
And Ms Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who came to this novel as a teenager and has never quite left it — she brings a reader's ear and a reader's heart.
Daniel, let's start with you — because Dickens opens the social world of this novel with one of the most extraordinary satirical conceits I've encountered in Victorian fiction.
He introduces Twemlow not as a man, but as a piece of furniture. What is Dickens doing there?
What Dickens is doing there is performing a diagnosis with surgical precision.
Twemlow is introduced as, and I want to be exact about the phrase here, 'an innocent piece of dinner-furniture that went upon easy castors.'
'an innocent piece of dinner-furniture that went upon easy castors and was kept over a livery stable-yard in Duke Street, Saint James's, when not in use.'
Not a man fallen on hard times. A dining table. Stored away when not required.
What makes it devastating is the logic that follows — the more Twemlow is 'pulled out,' the further he is from the centre of power.
His aristocratic connection — his first cousinship to Lord Snigsworth — is the very thing that makes him useful and the very thing that ensures his marginality.
The Veneerings need him precisely because they are new money performing old money, and he is the authenticating prop.
And the conceit is perfectly sustained — that's what makes it so remarkable as a piece of construction.
Dickens doesn't just introduce Twemlow as furniture and then drop the metaphor. He extends it through leaves, through centring, through distance from the head of the table.
The parallel holds, as Dickens himself says — and in that holding, it becomes almost unbearable.
Because Twemlow is innocent. The word is right there in the opening clause.
The satirical fury in this novel is almost always aimed at the guilty — the Veneerings, the Podsnaps, the Lammles. Twemlow is their victim.
What strikes me every time I read that passage is the specific address: Duke Street, Saint James's.
Dickens gives you a postcode for human humiliation. The very precision of it is the joke — and the cruelty.
And the line that stops me is the one Daniel quoted — the best quote in the passage.
'Being first cousin to Lord Snigsworth, he was in frequent requisition, and at many houses might be said to represent the dining-table in its normal state.'
The dining-table in its normal state. That is Twemlow's social function reduced to four words.
He is the baseline. The minimum. What you start with before the real guests arrive.
Now, this portrait of social parasitism and performance sits in interesting tension with what I'd call the novel's most genuinely tender passage — Boffin's account of young John Harmon.
Daniel, you've been assigned that passage too. It feels like a completely different emotional register.
It is a different register, and that contrast is precisely the point.
In the Veneering world, money transforms a man into furniture. In the Harmon world, the absence of money — or rather, the cruelty of those who hold it — transforms a child into an exile.
Old Harmon won't hear of allowing a sixpence of coach-money for the seven-year-old boy he's sending away alone.
That detail does more work than a paragraph of editorialising would. The father's wealth is measured in the coins he withholds from his son.
And then Dickens gives us Mrs Boffin. The passage Boffin narrates is almost unbearable in its warmth.
'Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks.'
The physicality of that — the two open hands, the kneeling, the warmth she is literally transferring to him — is everything the Veneering world has evacuated from human contact.
And then comes the line that haunts the whole novel for me.
'I'd give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!'
That repetition — the wide wide world — is Dickens writing in a folk register, almost a lullaby. And it breaks the heart precisely because she cannot run away with him.
That folk register is doing something architecturally important, I think.
Boffin's narration throughout this novel is rendered in a speech that is rough, unpretentious, phonetically rendered — 'pictur' for picture, 'year old' rather than 'years old.'
And yet what he describes has more moral grandeur than anything spoken in the Veneering drawing room.
Dickens is making a structural argument: the closer to the dust heap, the closer to genuine human feeling.
The Boffins are the hinge of that argument — good people to whom great wealth is suddenly given. Which is the novel's central test case.
I can never read that passage without stopping at the look the child gives them.
Boffin says the boy looks up at them 'as if it was in pain — in agony.' And then: 'Such a look!'
'he looks up at both of us, as if it was in pain—in agony. Such a look!'
Those two words — 'Such a look!' — are Boffin overwhelmed. Syntax collapsing under the weight of memory.
And what Mrs Boffin does with it — waking at night, calling out 'Don't you see the poor child's face?' — that's grief as a form of moral fidelity.
She refuses to let that look wear out. Until, as Boffin says with such quiet sadness, it 'gently wore out, as many things do.'
So we have the Boffins established as figures of genuine moral warmth — which makes what the novel then does with them so electrifying and so troubling.
Daniel, the novel doesn't confine its portrait of money's corruption to the upper classes. Wegg and Venus offer something darker, and I think funnier too.
Wegg is the novel's most complete portrait of what greed does to a person who has almost nothing to start with.
He is poor, he is disabled, he is barely literate — and yet money-hunger in him is as virulent as in any Veneering.
What Dickens gives us in the passage where Wegg and Venus react to news of hidden wealth is pure physical comedy — but it is comedy with a thesis.
The wooden leg elevates itself. Wegg nudges Venus deeper and deeper. He loses his balance entirely and collapses sideways.
'both remaining in a kind of pecuniary swoon.'
A pecuniary swoon. Three words that do the work of a satirical essay.
Greed as a physical intoxicant. The body given over entirely to the fantasy of money.
The genius of 'pecuniary swoon' is that it yokes a bureaucratic adjective to a romantic noun.
A swoon is what heroines do in sensation fiction. A pecuniary swoon is what Wegg does — and the collision is both ridiculous and precise.
Dickens is showing us that the emotional structure of romantic passion and the emotional structure of greed are — in Wegg — identical.
And it's funnier still because of the wooden leg.
The leg has its own trajectory — it elevates itself, almost independently. There's something of the cartoon about it.
But what makes me stop is the phrase 'some few seconds.' They don't immediately recover themselves.
They lie there together in their swoon, with Wegg squeezing Venus against the settle's edge, and neither of them minds. The money vision has abolished discomfort entirely.
That image of the alligator in Venus's shop watching all of this — that appears in another passage you've been assigned, Daniel.
Dickens uses the taxidermic specimens as a kind of sardonic Greek chorus. What's he reaching for there?
It's one of the novel's most startling passages, and it deserves to be read at length.
The narrator describes the French gentleman skeleton grinning, as if computing how many thousands of slanderers array themselves against the fortunate.
And then the alligator, whose yard or two of smile carries the most ancient verdict of all.
'the yard or two of smile on the part of the alligator might have been invested with the meaning,
All about this was quite familiar knowledge down in the depths of the slime, ages ago.
The alligator knows. It has always known. The transformation of benefactors into injurers is not a modern disease — it is as old as the slime itself.
What Dickens is doing is making the comedy of Wegg's greed suddenly vertiginous — zooming out to geological time.
The specimens are dead, preserved, displayed — and yet they are the most morally alert observers in the scene.
There's a grotesque wit in that which runs all through Venus's shop — the place where bodies are reassembled for display.
In a novel obsessed with identity and disguise — who is really John Harmon, what has Boffin really become — the articulator of bones is the perfect setting for moral revelation.
Disguise and revelation bring us neatly to what might be the novel's most elegantly constructed deception — and it connects directly to Twemlow, whom we met at the start.
Daniel, Mrs Lammle's revelation to Twemlow about Fledgeby and Riah — what does that passage expose about how money actually moves in this world?
It exposes the master structure of the novel's financial world: that visible agents are almost never the real ones.
Riah, the elderly Jewish moneylender, has been blamed — by Twemlow, by others — for the debts he pursues.
But Mrs Lammle's revelation is devastatingly simple.
'Mr Riah is his mask. It has fallen into Mr Fledgeby's hands.'
A mask. The word is exact and appalling. Fledgeby has weaponised a man — used him as a face for cruelty that he himself is too cowardly to wear openly.
And Mrs Lammle warns Twemlow not to judge another man's truthfulness by his own. It's almost unbearably pointed — because Twemlow is one of the novel's few genuinely honest men.
His very decency is the instrument of his victimisation. In this novel, goodness without knowledge is not safety — it is exposure.
Mrs Lammle herself is such an interesting figure at this moment.
She is herself a deceiver — she married Lammle under false pretences, as he married her. And yet here she is, delivering the truth.
Dickens is making a point about moral complexity that he rarely gets credited for: that people who know how deception works are sometimes the only ones who can dismantle it.
She fixes his eyes with hers — the narrator makes a point of noting that he cannot prevent her doing so, though he would if he could.
There is something almost forcible about her charity in this scene. She insists on saving him.
And the novel's portrait of complicity and exposure doesn't stop with the wealthy. Charley Hexam's confrontation with Bradley Headstone gives us something rawer.
Daniel, that passage is about guilt by association — about what happens when your ambition allies you with someone dangerous.
Charley Hexam is one of the novel's most uncomfortable creations — a boy who has clawed his way out of poverty and is terrified of being pulled back.
His confrontation with Bradley is entirely self-regarding. He doesn't accuse Bradley because the attack on Eugene was wrong. He accuses him because it has compromised Charley's own reputation.
Listen to how the accusation is structured — the hedging is deliberate and damning.
'If you had any part—I don't say what—in this attack, or if you know anything about it—I don't say how much—or if you know who did it—I go no closer.'
He goes no closer. He protects himself from the knowledge of what Bradley did, even as he punishes him for having done it.
And then the final line of the accusation: 'Is that your gratitude to me, Mr Headstone?'
'Is that your gratitude to me, Mr Headstone?'
Your gratitude to me. Not: you have done wrong. Not: you have hurt someone. Your gratitude to me. Charley's moral vocabulary has been entirely colonised by self-interest.
The hedging syntax is extraordinary craft — 'I don't say what,' 'I don't say how much,' 'I go no closer.'
Each qualification performs exactly the thing it claims to withhold. By saying 'I don't say what,' Charley says exactly what he means, while retaining deniability.
It is the rhetoric of a boy who has learned, in his rise, that language can be weaponised — and who has applied that lesson here with devastating effect.
What breaks me about Charley is what he represents for Lizzie.
She sacrificed for him. She let him have the education she was denied. And what education has made him is — this.
He accuses Bradley of laying him open to suspicion — 'Is that your gratitude to me?' — but the novel asks us to hear the same question echoing toward Charley himself.
What is Charley's gratitude to Lizzie? To the river? To the world that made him?
And that question — the debt we owe to those who made us and those we've used — runs through every one of these passages.
Twemlow the dining table, Mrs Boffin kneeling at the fire, Wegg in his pecuniary swoon, the alligator's ancient smile, Fledgeby's mask, Charley's chilling gratitude.
In each case, money isn't merely a backdrop — it is the active agent, dissolving or revealing the self that lies beneath.
My thanks to Eleanor, Daniel, and Caroline for a conversation that has left me wanting to read every one of these passages again immediately.
We'll be back shortly with the next segment.

segments.title: Bella's Reckoning: From Mercenary to Redeemed

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — as the strange, sprawling, brilliant thing it is.
I'm your host, and today we're deep inside one of the novel's most absorbing puzzles: the transformation of Bella Wilfer.
She begins the novel as a self-declared mercenary, furious at being left as a legacy in a dead man's will.
By its end, she has chosen love over money — but the path there is anything but simple, and Dickens makes it genuinely earned.
With me today are three people who bring very different eyes to this arc.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who is extraordinarily attentive to how Dickens constructs his effects — the architecture behind the apparent spontaneity.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads the novel as an anatomy of class power — and who will not let us sentimentalise Bella's story without asking who it costs.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens, and who has strong views about which characters deserve better from their author.
Let's begin with the mechanism Dickens sets in motion — John Harmon's secret scheme to observe Bella before she can know who he is.
What strikes me first about this scheme is how Dickens uses it structurally — it is essentially a test narrative embedded inside a larger one.
Harmon tells us exactly what he was after — he wanted to see Bella before she could know him for himself, and to give Mrs Boffin a glad surprise.
And then we get the plan in Harmon's own somewhat clinical words.
"the plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses, and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way"
That accumulation of gerund phrases — getting, throwing, trying — creates a kind of clumsy, improvisatory energy that perfectly suits the venture.
It's not a polished aristocratic plot — it's two men making it up as they go, which is exactly what makes it feel both comic and genuinely risky.
Eleanor is right that it reads as improvised — but let's be clear about what this improvisation actually is.
A wealthy man dresses as a common sailor in order to inspect a woman who has been assigned to him by inheritance, without her knowledge or consent.
The class transgression runs only one way — downward, and temporarily, and entirely on his terms.
Bella has no equivalent access to information about Harmon. She is surveilled. He is the surveyor.
Dickens gives us enough self-awareness in the prose to register this unease — but the novel never quite confronts it head-on.
Daniel's point is uncomfortable precisely because Dickens makes it so easy to enjoy the romance of the scheme.
And yet when we move into chapter thirty-one and Rokesmith revisits all of this in his own mind, the tone shifts completely.
There's a passage there I find genuinely moving — Dickens reaching into the psychology of self-deception with real precision.

"When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil — never yet for good within his knowledge then — of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few hours or days."
That long subordinate clause — the whole weight of his father's legacy pressing down before we even reach the main verb — that's Dickens showing us how the past buries intention.
Caroline, yes — that sentence is a masterclass in syntactic mirroring of psychological experience.
The accumulative power of separate circumstances — that's actually the narrator's phrase a few lines earlier — is enacted in the sentence structure itself.
And what makes the trap so devastating is the double bind Dickens constructs at the end.
By coming to life and accepting the inheritance, Harmon must buy Bella. By rejecting it, he must punish her.
There is no innocent move available to him. The money has pre-corrupted every possible action.
That double bind is real — and Eleanor is right that it's elegantly constructed.
But what I want to push on is Boffin's role in Bella's arc, because I think it's where Dickens is doing his most interesting — and most troubling — satirical work.
Consider what Boffin actually tells Bella about how she should live her life.
"Go in for money, my love. Money's the article. You'll make money of your good looks, and of the money Mrs Boffin and me will have the pleasure of settling upon you, and you'll live and die rich."
Dickens italicises that final word — rich — and renders it with a stutter: R—r—rich.
The satirical relish is unmistakeable. But the satire cuts in two directions — at Boffin, yes, but also at every version of Bella who found this advice appealing.
And that appeal is precisely what Bella has to reckon with in herself.
Let's talk about the moment of self-confrontation — and about the role Lizzie Hexam plays in forcing it.
The Bella and Lizzie scenes in chapter forty-two are, for me, among the most emotionally precise in the whole novel.
Bella is confronted by Lizzie's selflessness — by a form of love that simply does not register money as a category — and her response is to turn on herself.
And Dickens gives us this in the most wonderfully absurd, tender little action.
"There, you little mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain't you ashamed of your self?"
And she gives herself a penitential poke in the side.
It's comic, but it's also real shame. The comedy doesn't dilute the moral seriousness — it protects it from sentimentality.
That's a beautifully put distinction, Caroline — comedy as a prophylactic against sentimentality.
What's technically remarkable is that Bella's self-address is rendered in free indirect thought — Dickens makes us feel as though we are inside the self-rebuke.
The use of the second person — 'you little mercenary wretch' — creates an uncanny split: Bella is both the speaker and the accused.
That split is the transformation beginning. It requires a self that can stand apart from its own values and find them wanting.
I want to hold that thought alongside Lizzie's own words in the same chapter — because Lizzie is doing something quite specific here.
She is not moralising at Bella. She is simply telling the truth of her own experience.
Listen to how Lizzie describes her feeling for Eugene Wrayburn — a man who is her social superior and who has treated her with profound ambivalence.
"I would not have the light of them taken out of my life, for anything my life can give me."
The economy of that — light against life — is quietly extraordinary.
Lizzie is not asking to be loved back. She is not calculating return. She is simply asserting that this love has value precisely because it is given without condition.
For Bella, who has been calculating return her entire life, this is the most destabilising thing she could possibly hear.
And what moves me about Lizzie's confession is that last line — she had no thought of parting with any of it until the moment Bella came in.
Bella's presence unlocks something in Lizzie. That is itself a form of Bella's redemption being enacted rather than stated.
She has become the kind of person others trust with their most hidden feelings.
There's one more piece of this picture I want us to consider — Boffin's satirical outburst about charity and its patrons.
Because I think it sits right at the heart of what the novel believes about money, performance, and genuine virtue.
The charity passage is Dickens at his most gleefully satirical — and structurally it's doing important work adjacent to Bella's arc.
Boffin reads out this cascading list of titles — and the comedy is entirely in the accumulation.

"Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!"
The syntax mirrors the absurdity — each new prefix a new tier of meaningless distinction.
And the final image — Rokesmith sitting among the charity books pretty well up to his neck — turns institutional philanthropy into a slow drowning.
What Boffin's outburst reveals is the mechanism by which the wealthy launder moral credit.
Five shillings buys you a patronage title. The title signals virtue. The signalling substitutes for virtue.
This is exactly the world Bella is being trained to inhabit — the world in which appearance and money are the only currencies that count.
And it's Boffin who is doing the training — which is why his sudden performance of avarice works as a shock to her system.
And what Lizzie offers — wordlessly, without any moral programme — is the counter-image.
A love that gives without expecting a title. A life that measures itself by something other than wealth.
Bella's arc is, in a way, a slow movement from the charity-book world to Lizzie's world.
And Dickens is canny enough to make us feel the difficulty of that crossing rather than simply celebrating the arrival.
That notion of a difficult crossing — earned rather than bestowed — feels like the right place to pause this conversation.

What we've been tracing today is the architecture of a moral transformation: the surveillance that precedes it, the double bind that shapes it, the comic self-knowledge that begins it, and the counter-example that confirms it.
My thanks to Eleanor Hartley, Daniel Rosen, and Caroline Woodcourt for making Bella Wilfer feel new again.
We'll be back shortly with our next segment.
Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been tracing the novel's extraordinary range — its tenderness, its anger, its social conscience.
Now we turn to one of Dickens's most bravura gifts: the comic mask, and what hides behind it.
Our Mutual Friend is full of people performing versions of themselves — fraudulently, desperately, or brilliantly.
And Caroline Woodcourt, who has been reading this novel since she was a teenager, is exactly the right person to guide us through it.
Thank you — and I want to start with the Lammles, because Dickens does something almost unbearably knowing with them.
They put on this gorgeous performance of wedded contentment for their guests.
Smiles, tender looks, charming little interchanges — the whole theatre of a happy marriage.
And then the narrator leans in and says something that has made me laugh every single time I've read it.
"How delightful those interchanges, and the looks accompanying them! Now, if the skeleton up-stairs had taken that opportunity, for instance, of calling out 'Here I am, suffocating in the closet!'"
The skeleton in the closet — their ruinous fraud — is literally upstairs while they're performing marital bliss.
Dickens takes a tired idiom and makes it physically, grotesquely real.
That line is a masterclass in what I'd call the narrator's ironic omniscience.
He doesn't just know the secret — he invites the reader into the knowledge and then makes the performance visible as performance.
The exclamation mark in 'How delightful!' is doing double work — it mimics the approving social murmur and simultaneously exposes it as hollow.
That's a very sophisticated narratorial technique — free indirect style weaponised as satire.
And what the skeleton represents is worth being precise about.
The Lammles each married the other believing the other had money neither of them actually possessed.
Their entire social existence — the dinners, the clothes, the performance Caroline describes — is borrowed time on borrowed capital.
Dickens makes the marriage grotesque not because it's loveless, but because money is the only language respectable society speaks.
The skeleton suffocating in the closet is capitalism's dirty secret: the house of cards that gentility is built on.
I want to move to identity — because the novel is obsessed with people being not quite who they appear.
The passage where John Harmon removes his disguise is almost dizzying.
He strips away the oakum hair and whiskers, and becomes himself again — or rather, becomes one of his three selves.
Listen to what Dickens does with the repetition here.
"became as like that same lost wanted Mr Julius Handford, as never man was like another in this world."
And then — and this is the bit that astonishes me — he says the exact same thing about Rokesmith.
The phrase repeats verbatim, applied to a second identity, as if the novel itself is vertiginous with the multiplication of this man.
That verbal repetition is doing something structurally brilliant.
By repeating the formula word for word, Dickens performs the problem of identity rather than merely describing it.
We experience — as readers — the exact disorientation that the novel's mystery depends on.
Three names, one body, and the same sentence applied twice — it's a kind of formal joke that carries genuine existential weight.
It's also worth noting that Harmon's disguise is fundamentally about money and inheritance — he is performing poverty while being secretly rich.
The novel keeps asking: is your identity your name, your wealth, your face, or what you do?
Harmon, as the Secretary, works for his own inheritance without claiming it — he's testing whether the Boffins, and Bella, value him as a person or as a fortune.
And the comic masks aren't only worn by the wealthy or the mysterious.
There's a scene with the Deputy Lock and poor Betty Higden that is vicious comedy of a different order entirely.
He pockets her coins one by one while making this speech about his own virtue.
"I'm a man as earns his living by the sweat of his brow; and I won't stand in your way. Go where you like."
And Dickens notes that he drew his sleeve across his forehead — as if those pocketed coins were the result of virtuous industry.
The gap between the gesture and the deed — that's pure Dickens.
That scene makes me furious every time, and I mean that as the highest praise.
The Deputy Lock is a petty functionary of a system designed to make Betty Higden's desperation his opportunity.
He extorts the coins while performing the rhetoric of honest labour — which is precisely what the system asks of all its little enforcers.
The comedy is horrifying because the mask he's wearing is the mask the system issued him.
There's a very different kind of unmasking at the end of the novel, and it's almost physically satisfying.
Silas Wegg has been smirking and scheming and preening throughout, and then Harmon simply grabs him by the cravat.
The prose matches the action perfectly — short, percussive, almost gleeful.
"he found himself gripped by the cravat; shaken until his teeth chattered; shoved back, staggering, into a corner of the room; and pinned there."
Those semicolons — each one a fresh indignity — the rhythm enacts the shaking.
It's punctuation as slapstick.
And just before that, the Secretary's warning to Wegg is perfectly calibrated — comic, but with real menace underneath.
He throws something out of the room first, then turns and says:
"Be careful what insolent liberties you take in that gentleman's presence, or I will throw you after it."
It's the understatement that makes it so funny — and so satisfying.
Wegg has been getting away with his little performances for so long, and suddenly the mask of genteel tolerance is simply gone.
Masks worn and masks torn away — that's the heartbeat of this novel's comedy, and you've all brought it to life wonderfully.
From the Lammles' drawing room to Wegg's flying cravat, Dickens uses laughter to expose exactly what polite society would rather keep upstairs.
In our next segment, we'll be turning to the novel's river — its most powerful and ambiguous symbol.

segments.title: Society's Margins: The Poor and the Polluted

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart — passage by passage, character by character — to find out what it's really doing.

I'm your host, and today we're deep into the world of the Boffins — the Golden Dustman and his wife, suddenly catastrophically rich, and the entire ecosystem of exploitation that springs up around them.
Our segment is called Society's Margins: The Poor and the Polluted — and we're asking what Dickens is actually saying about charity, class, and the uses of wealth.
With me are three wonderful readers of this novel.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who cares passionately about how fiction is built — the architecture of sentences, the mechanics of satire.
Dr Daniel Rosen reads novels as anatomies of class power — and he argues that Dickens was more radical than he himself knew.
And Ms Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has re-read this novel many times and brings an extraordinary sensitivity to what it actually feels like to read it, sentence by sentence.
Let's begin with the flood — the extraordinary catalogue of charity appeals that descends on Boffin the moment his fortune becomes public knowledge.
What strikes me first about this passage is the sheer structural audacity of it — Dickens is essentially writing a satirical taxonomy.
He doesn't give us one begging letter; he gives us an entire typology — churches, parsonages, organs, children on postage stamps.
The accumulation is the joke, but it's also the argument: the whole system of Victorian organised charity is being indicted at once.
And then Dickens does something really precise — he zooms in on one letter and gives it to us in full.
He sets it up with this magnificently deadpan detail:
"Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet."
That sentence is doing enormous work in six words — the physical bulk of the letter, the self-important privacy, the aristocratic seal.
Dickens has compressed an entire social performance into one noun phrase.
Eleanor is absolutely right about the compression — but I want to press on what the target actually is here.
Because the Duke of Linseed isn't simply pompous — he's operating a mechanism.
The charity dinner exists to launder the aristocracy's social legitimacy by association with new money — and new money pays three guineas for the privilege.
And Dickens makes sure we see the machinery exposed — the letter is, as he tells us, lithographed by the hundred.
"Presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand."
The personal warmth — 'My Dear Sir,' the Duke's faithful service — is mass-produced.
This is Dickens anatomising what we might now call the charity-industrial complex — and he does it with ice-cold precision.
What I love — and I use that word carefully — is the way Dickens performs the very thing he's satirising.
He gives us the Duke's letter in full, with all its flattery and its pointed postscript about the three guineas.
And then he adds, with beautiful restraint: "Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of Linseed — and thoughtful in the postscript."
That dry little parenthesis is everything — the narrator winking at us without ever dropping his composure.
I've re-read this passage many times, and that aside never stops being funny.
That restraint is doing a lot of work — and it modulates into something darker when we move to the individual beggars, the non-institutional ones.
Because that passage has a very different emotional texture — comic on the surface, but something more unsettling underneath.
Yes — and this is where I find myself pulling up short as a reader.
The comedy is real — the inspired beggars, sitting over their fragment of candle while an Angel whispers Boffin's name — it's wonderfully absurd.
But these are people in genuine desperate poverty.
Dickens catches the texture of their desperation — the cold potato, the rent in arrear, the heartless landlady threatening expulsion like a dog.
And then there's that line about their documents — it just stops me every time.
"They call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf."
That comparison is savage and funny and, when you sit with it, almost unbearably sad.
Their proof of identity, their evidence of existence, reduced to something that has already been ground up and made unrecognisable.
Caroline has put her finger on the thing that makes this passage more than satire — it's also a diagnosis.
Look at the range of people catalogued here: daughters of army officers, spouses hiding from each other, people threatening suicide by the quarter hour.
What Dickens is showing us is a society that has produced massive destitution and has no legitimate structural response to it.
The only resource available to these people is to perform poverty before a single wealthy man — and to be funny or pathetic enough to catch his attention.
The beggars on horseback — the ones who need an astronomical telescope to reach prosperity — are particularly sharp.
They have absorbed every piece of Victorian self-help ideology — the goal is before them, the road is in the best condition — and it has brought them to complete paralysis.
The ideology that was supposed to liberate them has instead furnished them with a more elaborate language for their failure.
Daniel's point about the catalogue is crucial to understanding the craft here as well.
Dickens organises the individual beggars into named categories — the inspired beggars, the nobly independent beggars, the beggars of punctual business-habits.
It's a mock-taxonomy — imitating the rational, systematic language of the age's social science — and it makes the whole thing more grotesque by being so methodical.
And notice that the Secretary is the consciousness through which all of this passes — 'how does the heart of the Secretary fail him.'
Dickens gives us a bureaucrat with a heart — and then floods that heart with an impossible volume of human misery to process.
It's a structural choice that keeps the comedy from collapsing into mere cruelty.
And yet Boffin himself — the object of all this attention — has his own ambiguous relationship to the wealth that makes him so magnetic.
We have that marvellous passage where Dickens describes him settling into the mansion — and the image he reaches for is one of the most compressed in the whole novel.
The cheese simile — I think about it every time I walk past a grand London terrace.
Dickens writes that Boffin's mansion was,
"like an eminently aristocratic family cheese, it was much too large for his wants, and bred an infinite amount of parasites."
The audacity of that — comparing a London mansion to a cheese — is one of Dickens's most characteristic moves.
He deflates the grandeur and the aspiration in one absurd domestic image.
But the word 'parasites' is doing something else entirely — it isn't just funny, it's a verdict.
All those beggars and charity organisers and dukes writing lithographed letters — they are the organisms that wealth of this kind necessarily generates.
And the opening of that paragraph is worth attending to as well — Dickens calls Boffin 'the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour.'
"The minion of fortune and the worm of the hour, or in less cutting language, Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, the Golden Dustman."
That 'or in less cutting language' is a beautiful piece of self-commentary — the narrator flagging his own sharpness and then pretending to soften it.
Boffin is simultaneously a sympathetic character and a symbol of the arbitrary cruelty of how wealth is distributed.
He didn't earn his money in any meaningful sense — he was a servant who inherited through the logic of a will.
Which brings us to that extraordinary document Wegg unearths — the will that leaves 'the Little Mound' to Boffin, and everything else to the Crown.
That will — when Wegg reads it out — is one of the most chilling comic moments in the novel, I think.
Wegg delivers it with that extraordinary self-satisfied theatrical energy — 'Hear, hear, hear!'
And then the will itself — read aloud as if it's a triumph — says the bleakest possible things about old Harmon.

"Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown."
'Never made friends.' 'Has ever had a rebellious family.' The will reads like an epitaph for a failed life.
And yet out of that bitterness — those dust heaps, that isolation — the whole novel grows.
And that phrase 'quite enough for him' — I find it devastating.
It's the voice of a man who resented everyone and trusted no one — dispensing his fortune with a contempt so thorough it extends to generosity.
And then Wegg — Wegg of all people — gets hold of this document and promptly uses it to fuel his own small, ugly appetite for power.
Which is where the novel makes its most pointed observation about what power does to base natures.
The Wegg passage about hovering over Boffin's house is — I'll say it plainly — one of the great short analyses of power in the Victorian novel.
Dickens writes — and I want to read this carefully because the phrasing is precise:
"Power — unless it be the power of intellect or virtue — has ever the greatest attraction for the lowest natures."
That parenthesis — 'unless it be the power of intellect or virtue' — is crucial.
Dickens is not saying all power corrupts — he's making a class distinction about the kinds of power available to men like Wegg.
Wegg has no wealth, no intellect worth speaking of, no social position — what he has is a secret.
And the novel shows us with horrible clarity exactly what a man of Wegg's formation does with that tiny fragment of destructive power.
He hovers.
'He hovers' — and Dickens gives that hovering such a perfect image.
Wegg fantasises about his power to strip the roof off the inhabiting family — and Dickens renders this:
"The mere defiance of the unconscious house-front, with his power to strip the roof off the inhabiting family like the roof of a house of cards, was a treat which had a charm for Silas Wegg."
'A treat which had a charm' — Dickens's irony is at its most devastating there.
Wegg's private pleasure in imagined destruction — the cosiness of it, the snugness — is rendered with the language of a child's reward.
It's the novel's most frightening portrait of petty malice.

Petty malice, systemic charity fraud, ducal condescension, and the destitute with their 'minced veal' documents — this novel covers the entire vertical range of Victorian society, and finds it all wanting.
Thank you all — Eleanor, Daniel, Caroline — for a conversation that has, I think, shown us how much Dickens packs into what might initially look like comic set-pieces.
Next, we'll be turning to the river itself — what it means, what it carries, and the people whose lives are shaped by what it yields.

segments.title: Narrative Games: How Dickens Plays the Reader

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
I'm your host, and today we're diving into something that Dickens does with extraordinary cunning throughout this novel: the way he plays the reader.
Disguises, delayed revelations, narrators who know more than they're letting on — this is a book that treats readerly trust as something to be earned, tested, and occasionally betrayed.
With me today are three brilliant readers of this novel, each bringing a distinct lens.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who is fascinated by how Dickens constructs his effects — the architecture beneath the surface of the prose.
Dr Daniel Rosen reads every narrative choice as an act of ideology — who the novel sees, who it hides, and what that concealment serves.
And Ms Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel for decades and brings the irreplaceable perspective of a reader who has felt every one of its shocks and pleasures.
Let's begin with the question of what it means for Dickens to hide things — not just from characters, but from us.
What I find endlessly fascinating about this novel's narrative design is that Dickens isn't simply withholding information — he's engineering misdirection at the level of the sentence.
Take Eugene Wrayburn, who is in some ways the novel's most self-aware character — and therefore its most confounding.
Lightwood tries to push him toward introspection — 'Look on to the end' — and Dickens gives us this extraordinary moment of arrested self-knowledge.
Eugene simply says: 'That's exactly what I am incapable of doing.'
And it's devastating — not because it's a cry for help, but because it's delivered with almost clinical detachment.
The narrator tells us he says it 'with a perplexed and inquisitive face, as if he actually did not know what to make of himself.'
Dickens is using Eugene's opacity to mirror our own — we can't plan ahead in this novel because the novel won't let us.
Eugene is essentially a structural metaphor for Dickens's own narrative strategy.
That's a beautiful formulation, Eleanor, but I want to push on it slightly — because I think the hiding operates differently depending on whose story is being concealed.
Harmon's disguise, for instance, is a narrative game that Dickens plays entirely on behalf of someone with money.
And look at how that game is finally revealed — Harmon confronting Wegg, with this magnificent contempt.

He tells him: 'I tell you this, that you may know we knew enough of you to persuade Mr Boffin to let us lead you on, deluded, to the last possible moment, in order that your disappointment might be the heaviest possible disappointment.'
This is the novel's deception made explicit — and it's ruthless.
They didn't merely catch Wegg — they engineered his maximum humiliation.
The narrative withholds this information from us for the same reason: our satisfaction is purchased at the cost of our complicity in the trap.
What strikes me reading all of this is how viscerally the narrator involves us — not just as witnesses to deception, but as its targets.
There's a passage about Bradley Headstone that I keep returning to — because it's not about plot at all, it's about the torment of a mind Dickens has refused to let us enter cleanly.
The narrator says — and I want to read this carefully —
'He had no remorse; but the evildoer who can hold that avenger at bay, cannot escape the slower torture of incessantly doing the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently.'
There's no remorse — and yet there is something worse than remorse.
Dickens denies Bradley the dignity of guilt and denies us the comfort of a repentant villain.
That is a very uncomfortable place to leave a reader.
Caroline, yes — and I think that connects directly to the novel's use of motion, of kinetic imagery, to evade the reader's grasp.
There's an extraordinary passage where the train crosses the river — and it's not a description, it's an assault.
Listen to the syntax here:

'the train rattled among the house-tops, and among the ragged sides of houses torn down to make way for it, and over the swarming streets, and under the fruitful earth, until it shot across the river: bursting over the quiet surface like a bomb-shell, and gone again as if it had exploded in the rush of smoke and steam and glare.'
That accumulating 'and... and... and...' is a sentence that mimics the train itself — it will not let you stop.
And then it's gone — 'gone again as if it had exploded.'
The reader is left with smoke.
I love that reading, but I want to add something: that train is also destroying things.
The 'ragged sides of houses torn down to make way for it' — that's not poetic licence, that's the literal violence of Victorian railway expansion on working-class neighbourhoods.
The narrator compares the train to Father Time — 'going straight to its end, as Father Time goes to his' — and for the poor, Father Time is rarely gentle.
The narrative game here is one of sublime aestheticisation — Dickens makes the machine beautiful precisely at the moment it is most destructive.
That is a narrative choice that rewards interrogation.
I want to bring us back to something earthier — to Mr Boffin, who is arguably the novel's greatest narrative trick played on the reader's sympathies.
There's a passage early in the novel where Boffin is telling Mortimer Lightwood about the old man's cruelty to young John Harmon — and about how he and Mrs Boffin tried to protect him.
And Boffin describes old Harmon's rages — in this voice that is somehow both comic and completely harrowing:

'I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet (she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head), and send it spinning across the yard.'
And then the sentence that drops the floor from under you:
'Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her.'
That repetition — 'Dropped her' — is devastating in its simplicity.
The comedy of the bonnet is exactly calibrated to make the violence land harder.
That is Dickens's most ruthless trick as a narrator: making us laugh so that the blow lands on us too.
And Boffin's voice — that dialect, that guileless syntax — is doing double duty.
It's the voice of a man who cannot dress up horror — who can only report it directly, without ornament.
And Dickens uses that ingenuousness as a kind of narrative clearance — it strips away all the novel's elaborate games and gives us something raw.
And notice who is hearing this story: Mortimer Lightwood, a man of the professional class, trained in law, in rhetoric, in social performance.
Boffin is the witness of the suffering, but he has to deliver that testimony to someone whose world produced the conditions for it.
The novel's most piercing narrative trick is not the Harmon disguise, not the Boffin transformation — it's this: that the poor carry the truth, but the plot belongs to the rich.
That is a genuinely arresting note to pause on.
The poor carry the truth, but the plot belongs to the rich — it feels like a verdict on the novel, and also perhaps on the form itself.
In our next segment, we'll be looking at the novel's great comic creation — and asking whether comedy, in Dickens, is ever really just comedy.
We've been circling, throughout this episode, the question of what redemption actually costs in this novel.
Not redemption as a gift — but as something earned, tested, sometimes disguised.
These final passages bring us to the heart of that question — Bella's transformation, and the extraordinary lengths taken to provoke it.
Eleanor, I'd like to start with you, because the architecture here is genuinely audacious.
It really is audacious — and it requires us to sit with something quite uncomfortable.
John Harmon decides, from a sickbed in a public house, to remain dead.
He decides to use near-murder as an instrument of moral experiment.
The passage gives us the precise moment of that decision, and Dickens frames it with extraordinary self-awareness.
John Harmon says, in his own voice:
"the thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella."
That word — proving — carries enormous weight.
She is not being loved. She is being tested. And Dickens makes sure we feel the difference.
And notice what the test is actually for — it's not about Bella's virtue in any abstract sense.
It's about what she will do in the presence of money.
The passage is quite explicit — the fear driving John is the fate of his father's riches.
The wealth that "should lead to nothing but evil."
So the novel stages it beautifully — Mr Boffin performs corruption to expose Bella's susceptibility to it.
And we see exactly what that corruption looks like from the outside.
Bella catches it — steals a glance and sees what the novel calls
"a dark cloud of suspicion, covetousness, and conceit, overshadowing the once open face."
The face that was once open is now closed by wealth. That's the system made visible in a single physiognomy.
What I keep returning to is how that moment with Mr Boffin is filtered through Bella's eyes — through her eyelashes, almost furtively.
She's learning to read the world more honestly, and it costs her something to look.
And then there's that passage with Rokesmith watching her from the doorway — which breaks my heart every time.
The language is doing something so precise here. Let me read it:

"The Secretary looked on from a doorway at the boofer lady thus encircled, and still looked on at the boofer lady standing alone there, when the determined old figure with its steady bright eyes was trudging through the streets, away from paralysis and pauperism."
He's still called "the Secretary" — not John, not Rokesmith by name — at the very moment he's watching the woman he loves.
The disguise is built into the grammar of the sentence. He can't reach her yet.
That's exactly right — and notice how the repetition of "boofer lady" does something structurally essential.
The first time, she's encircled — held by Betty, by connection, by warmth.
The second time, she's standing alone. The same phrase, two entirely different emotional worlds.
Dickens uses that verbal echo to make the isolation audible, almost like a musical motif resolving to silence.
And Betty Higden is trudging away — away from paralysis and pauperism, the novel says.
Those aren't decorative words. That's the workhouse. That's the Poor Law.
What I find remarkable is how Dickens holds all of this in a single image — the watching man, the solitary woman, the fleeing old figure.
Class, love, and the terror of institutional death — all in one sentence.
And what redeems the novel, finally, is that connection does come — Bella does choose John without knowing his fortune.
She passes the test. But I always feel the novel is honest enough to show us the cost of designing such a test in the first place.
John's fear — that the money would lead to nothing but evil — is not irrational.
He grew up inside that damage. And the novel never quite lets him off the hook for inflicting a version of it onto her.
That tension — between the necessity of the test and the cruelty of administering it — feels like the moral centre Dickens is always pressing on.
Eleanor, Daniel, Caroline — this has been a genuinely illuminating conversation, and I think we've only begun to account for what this novel carries.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel that watches its characters from doorways — always slightly hidden, always probing — and it seems to me that's exactly what great fiction does.
Thank you for joining us on Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.

‘The last time me and Mrs Boffin saw the poor boy,’ said Mr Boffin,
      warming (as fat usually does) with a tendency to melt, ‘he was a child of
      seven year old. For when he came back to make intercession for his sister,
      me and Mrs Boffin were away overlooking a country contract which was to be
      sifted before carted, and he was come and gone in a single hour. I say he
      was a child of seven year old. He was going away, all alone and forlorn,
      to that foreign school, and he come into our place, situate up the yard of
      the present Bower, to have a warm at our fire. There was his little scanty
      travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in
      the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the
      steamboat, as the old man wouldn’t hear of allowing a sixpence
      coach-money. Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a
      full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two
      open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks; but seeing the tears come
      into the child’s eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him
      round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, “I’d
      give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!” I don’t say but
      what it cut me, and but what it at the same time heightened my feelings of
      admiration for Mrs Boffin. The poor child clings to her for awhile, as she
      clings to him, and then, when the old man calls, he says “I must go! God
      bless you!” and for a moment rests his heart against her bosom, and looks
      up at both of us, as if it was in pain—in agony. Such a look! I went
      aboard with him (I gave him first what little treat I thought he’d like),
      and I left him when he had fallen asleep in his berth, and I came back to
      Mrs Boffin. But tell her what I would of how I had left him, it all went
      for nothing, for, according to her thoughts, he never changed that look
      that he had looked up at us two. But it did one piece of good. Mrs Boffin
      and me had no child of our own, and had sometimes wished that how we had
      one. But not now. “We might both of us die,” says Mrs Boffin, “and other
      eyes might see that lonely look in our child.” So of a night, when it was
      very cold, or when the wind roared, or the rain dripped heavy, she would
      wake sobbing, and call out in a fluster, “Don’t you see the poor child’s
      face? O shelter the poor child!”—till in course of years it gently
      wore out, as many things do.’

He went over it all again. He had lapsed into the condition in which he
      found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without
      perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances. When in
      the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never
      yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his
      father’s wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of
      his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few
      hours or days, it was to involve in it only the girl so capriciously
      forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was
      honestly meant well towards her. For, if he had found her unhappy in the
      prospect of that marriage (through her heart inclining to another man or
      for any other cause), he would seriously have said: ‘This is another of
      the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go to my
      and my sister’s only protectors and friends.’ When the snare into which he
      fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded
      by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly
      accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it
      must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune. When he
      saw them, and knew them, and even from his vantage-ground of inspection
      could find no flaw in them, he asked himself, ‘And shall I come to life to
      dispossess such people as these?’ There was no good to set against the
      putting of them to that hard proof. He had heard from Bella’s own lips
      when he stood tapping at the door on that night of his taking the
      lodgings, that the marriage would have been on her part thoroughly
      mercenary. He had since tried her, in his own unknown person and supposed
      station, and she not only rejected his advances but resented them. Was it
      for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?
      Yet, by coming to life and accepting the condition of the inheritance, he
      must do the former; and by coming to life and rejecting it, he must do the
      latter.

These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?

      claims of the nat’ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin’s bonnet (she wore,
      in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top

      once, when he did this in a manner that amounted to personal, I should

‘I have checked the calculation often, and it must have been two nights
      that I lay recovering in that public-house. Let me see. Yes. I am sure it
      was while I lay in that bed there, that the thought entered my head of
      turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some
      time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella. The
      dread of our being forced on one another, and perpetuating the fate that
      seemed to have fallen on my father’s riches—the fate that they
      should lead to nothing but evil—was strong upon the moral timidity
      that dates from my childhood with my poor sister.

      and still looked on at the boofer lady standing alone there, when the
      determined old figure with its steady bright eyes was trudging through the
      streets, away from paralysis and pauperism.
